figures.sourceHeading: The reaction between methane and bromine in the presence of ultraviolet radiation

specPoints.text: describe the reactions of alkanes with halogens in the presence of ultraviolet radiation, limited to mono-substitution knowledge of reaction mechanisms is not required

primer.text: From Alkanes you already know this family is generally unreactive, with halogen chemistry listed as one of its few moves. This note runs that move in detail: what ultraviolet light unlocks, the equations for methane with bromine and chlorine, and the halogenoalkane products that follow.

lessons.title: Swapping atoms under UV light
sourceHeadings: The reaction between methane and bromine in the presence of ultraviolet radiation
lessons.opening: Left alone, an alkane ignores a halogen. Switch on ultraviolet light and a hydrogen atom is swapped for a halogen atom in a reaction whose shape this lesson maps out.
keyPoints: A substitution reaction swaps one atom in a molecule for another atom.
Alkanes react with halogens only in the presence of ultraviolet radiation.
Methane plus bromine under UV gives bromomethane and hydrogen bromide: CH4 + Br2 -> CH3Br + HBr.
The same pattern with chlorine gives chloromethane and hydrogen chloride: CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl.
The substitution here is limited to mono-substitution, one halogen atom per methane molecule.

low.restatement: With UV light on, a halogen atom trades places with a hydrogen on the alkane. Methane gives bromomethane plus HBr with bromine, or chloromethane plus HCl with chlorine. Only one swap happens per molecule at this level, and the light supplies the trigger that makes it possible.
low.analogy: Ultraviolet light is the referee who lets the substitution match begin; without the whistle, both teams stand still.
low.examPointer: Always state the UV condition; the reaction does not proceed appreciably without it.

medium.restatement: Alkanes undergo substitution with halogens under ultraviolet light, one atom at a time as far as mono-substitution. Methane and bromine yield bromomethane and hydrogen bromide, while chlorine under the same conditions yields chloromethane and hydrogen chloride, each equation pairing the haloalkane with the hydrogen halide.
medium.analogy: Picture a dance floor where UV is the music: only when it plays does one hydrogen dancer leave the floor and a halogen take the vacant place, one swap per song.
medium.examPointer: Write both products, the haloalkane and the hydrogen halide, and mark the reaction as mono-substitution if asked to limit it.

check.stem: What condition is required for methane to react with bromine?

options.explanation: UV light is the trigger that allows the substitution to run.
Those are cracking conditions; this reaction needs light, not that furnace.
Oxygen belongs to combustion; this substitution needs none.

options.text: No condition is needed at all
options.explanation: In the dark the alkane and halogen simply coexist.

check.stem: Which products form when methane reacts with bromine under UV light?

options.explanation: The swap makes CH3Br and pairs the displaced hydrogen with the remaining bromine as HBr.
That is the combustion product pair; no oxygen appears here.
Dibromo products come from alkene addition, a different family and reaction.
Methanol belongs to the alcohol family and chlorine never enters this reaction.

check.stem: Why is this reaction classified as substitution?

options.text: Because a hydrogen atom on the alkane is replaced by a halogen atom
options.explanation: One-for-one replacement is the defining signature of substitution.

options.text: Because two molecules merge into one product
options.explanation: Merging describes addition, and here two products form.

options.text: Because the alkane burns in the halogen
options.explanation: Burning requires oxygen; halogens are not oxygen.

options.text: Because the molecules merely mix without reacting
options.explanation: New substances with new bonds form, so a genuine reaction has occurred.

check.stem: What does mono-substitution limit in this reaction?

options.text: Only one halogen atom replaces a hydrogen per methane molecule
options.explanation: The specification limits the treatment to a single swap, giving CH3Br rather than multi-brominated products.

options.text: Only one reaction may happen per container
options.explanation: The limit describes the molecule, not laboratory logistics.

options.text: Only methane may take part, ever
options.explanation: Other alkanes also undergo the substitution; the limit is about swap count.

options.text: Only one UV photon is allowed per second
options.explanation: Light intensity is not what mono-substitution describes.

check.stem: Which name describes the family of products such as bromomethane and chloromethane?

options.explanation: The note names the product family halogenoalkanes or haloalkanes.
Alkenes carry C=C double bonds; the products here are single-bonded.
Alcohols carry the OH group, not a halogen atom.
No acid group forms in this substitution.

lessons.title: Haloalkanes and their uses
lessons.opening: The products of alkane substitution are not laboratory curiosities; they run freezers, inhalers and solvents. This lesson follows the chlorine example and the CFC story behind the product family.
keyPoints: Chlorine reacts with alkanes under the same UV conditions to form chloromethane.
Methane plus chlorine gives CH3Cl and HCl by the same substitution pattern as bromine.
Both products sit in a family the note names halogenoalkanes, or haloalkanes for short.
Halogenoalkanes see use as solvents, refrigerants, propellants and pharmaceuticals.
CFCs are chlorofluorocarbons, family members now phased out because they harm the ozone layer.

low.restatement: Chlorine does the same job as bromine, swapping onto methane to give chloromethane and HCl. The products form a useful family called halogenoalkanes, seen in solvents and old fridges.
low.analogy: Swap the halogen and you swap the flavour of the product, like the same recipe baked with different spice; the family name just records which halogen came to visit.
low.examPointer: Quote one use of halogenoalkanes and the CFC-ozone story if the question stretches to applications.

medium.restatement: Under ultraviolet light chlorine substitutes onto methane exactly as bromine does, giving chloromethane and hydrogen chloride. Both products sit in the halogenoalkane family, valued as solvents, refrigerants, propellants and pharmaceuticals, though the chlorofluorocarbon members were phased out for ozone damage.
medium.analogy: The haloalkane family is a toolbox where the halogen is the handle: swap bromine for chlorine and the tool changes job, from solvent to refrigerant, while the carbon skeleton stays the same.
medium.examPointer: Link the UV condition to both halogens, then answer use questions with the four listed roles or the CFC ozone story.

check.stem: Balance the chlorine substitution: CH4 + Cl2 -> ?

options.explanation: One chlorine joins the carbon, and the displaced hydrogen pairs with the other chlorine as HCl.
That is a double substitution beyond the mono-substitution limit of this treatment.
Full substitution is excluded here and the hydrogen product form is wrong.
The displaced hydrogen must appear as the second product, hydrogen chloride.

check.stem: Which of these is a listed use of halogenoalkanes?

options.explanation: The note lists solvents, refrigerants, propellants and pharmaceuticals.
Roads take bitumen, a crude oil fraction, not halogenoalkanes.
Jet fuel is kerosene from the fraction ladder.
Fertilisers belong to nitrogen chemistry, not haloalkane uses.

check.stem: What does CFC stand for, and why were CFCs phased out?

options.text: Chlorofluorocarbon, phased out for ozone layer damage
options.explanation: The exam hint names the class and the ozone-layer reason for the phase-out.

options.text: Carbon fuel cell, phased out for inefficiency
options.explanation: The letters spell a halogenoalkane class, not a fuel cell device.

options.text: Chlorofluorocarbon, phased out for costing too much
options.explanation: Cost was never the recorded reason; ozone damage was.
CFCs are compounds containing chlorine and fluorine, not the raw gas.

check.stem: Why do bromine and chlorine react with methane in the same pattern?

options.text: Both are halogens and substitute one hydrogen under UV light
options.explanation: The halogen family chemistry transfers: one swap, one haloalkane, one hydrogen halide.

options.text: Because both are metals with similar ions
options.explanation: Halogens are non-metals; the shared pattern comes from their family chemistry.
Noble gases barely react at all; halogens are the reactive family here.

options.text: Because methane forces every reagent into addition
options.explanation: Methane has no double bond, so addition cannot happen; substitution is the route.

check.stem: A student shines visible red light on methane and bromine and sees no reaction. What explains this?

options.text: The substitution specifically needs ultraviolet radiation, not visible light
options.explanation: The condition of record is ultraviolet; other light lacks the energy trigger the reaction needs.

options.text: The gases must first be dissolved in water
options.explanation: No solution step is part of this reaction.

options.text: Bromine is too unreactive to react with anything
options.explanation: Bromine reacts readily once the UV condition is met.

options.text: The reaction happened but was invisible
options.explanation: The colour change as bromine is consumed would be visible had it reacted.

glossary.definition: A reaction in which one atom in a molecule is swapped for another atom.
A Group 7 element such as bromine or chlorine that can substitute onto alkanes under UV light.
An alkane derivative carrying one or more halogen atoms, also called a haloalkane.
The limit in which only one halogen atom replaces a hydrogen on each alkane molecule.
A halogenoalkane containing chlorine and fluorine, formerly used in fridges and now phased out for ozone damage.

workedExample.prompt: a) State the condition needed for methane to react with bromine. b) Write the equations for methane reacting with bromine and with chlorine, naming the products. c) What does mono-substitution limit, and which product family results?
steps: a) Ultraviolet radiation — alkanes react with halogens only in the presence of UV light.
b) CH4 + Br2 → CH3Br + HBr (bromomethane + hydrogen bromide); CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl (chloromethane + hydrogen chloride).
c) Mono-substitution limits the reaction to one halogen atom replacing one hydrogen on each alkane molecule; the haloalkane products belong to the halogenoalkane family.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Ultraviolet radiation. b) CH4 + Br2 → CH3Br + HBr; CH4 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + HCl. c) One halogen swap per molecule; halogenoalkanes.
